title: Location data enables movement tracking and user profiling
description: GPS position and timestamps in the data flow can be used to link the user's movements over time, enabling detailed location tracking and behavioral profiling even without direct identification.

title: Sensor telemetry can identify user through biometric patterns
description: Heart rate and step count data combined with timestamps can be used to identify the specific user through unique biometric patterns and activity signatures.

title: Data in transit vulnerable to interception
description: Sensor telemetry transmitted from wearable device to processing system may be intercepted by unauthorized parties during transmission.

title: Wearable device may store sensitive health data insecurely
description: The wearable device (Process P1) receives and processes sensitive health and location data, creating risk of unauthorized access or improper storage.

title: Continuous monitoring may exceed user consent scope
description: The act of wearing the device and sharing continuous sensor telemetry may involve data collection beyond what the user explicitly consented to.

title: Explicit Data Disclosure via Device-to-App Sync
description: The wearable device explicitly transfers personal data (GPS traces, device id, timestamps, exercise sessions) to the companion app by design. This represents an intentional disclosure of personal data across a system boundary, which may be avoidable if minimality principles are not followed.

title: Linkability via GPS Traces and Device Metadata
description: GPS traces combined with device id and timestamps in transit can be used to link the user's location history to their identity, potentially enabling tracking across different contexts or systems.

title: Identifiability Through Device ID and Location Data
description: The device id and GPS traces transferred in the data flow can be used to identify the specific user, especially when combined with timestamps that create a unique behavioral fingerprint.

title: Source Element Shares Excessive Personal Data
description: The wearable device (P1) shares personal data (GPS traces, device id, timestamps) with the companion app. The threat arises from the act of sharing at the source, where data minimality may not be respected.

title: Identification via data in transit
description: Calorie, meal, and weight data transmitted between user and app could be intercepted and used to identify the user's health profile and habits.

title: Linkability of health data
description: Data in transit could be linked with other data sources to create a comprehensive health profile of the user.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of health data
description: The companion app could disclose user's calorie, meal, and weight data to third parties without consent.

title: Data degradation or alteration
description: The app could alter or degrade the accuracy of logged health data during processing or storage.

title: Explicit Location Data Disclosure to Storage
description: The Companion Mobile App explicitly transfers GPS location traces with timestamps to the Location History Store. This constitutes an explicit data disclosure where personal location data is transferred across a boundary and stored. The minimality principle is at risk - the disclosure may not be strictly necessary for the intended purpose, and storing detailed location history creates long-term privacy risks.
assumptions: Location data is considered personal data under privacy regulations; the store retains data beyond immediate processing needs.

title: Linkability of Location Traces via Timestamps
description: GPS location traces with timestamps in transit could be used to link different data points or activities to a specific individual. The temporal and spatial precision of location data enables correlation across time periods, potentially revealing patterns of movement, routines, and associations.
assumptions: Location data with timestamps can be correlated with other data sources or used to infer sensitive information about the user's activities and associations.

title: Identification Risk from Location Data Sharing
description: The act of sharing GPS location traces with timestamps from the Companion Mobile App creates identification risk. Precise location data can be used to identify individuals, especially when combined with timestamps that reveal when and where the user was present. This identification may occur even without additional identifiers.
assumptions: Location data alone can be sufficient for identification in many contexts; the app shares data without adequate anonymization.

title: Unintended Health Data Disclosure During Analytics Processing
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise logs) transferred across sessions for health-condition analysis may disclose more personal information than strictly necessary. The analytics service could derive or infer additional health conditions beyond the intended analysis scope, violating the minimality principle.

title: Linkability of Health Data Across Sessions
description: Metadata or patterns in the transferred health logs could be used to link data across different sessions, potentially revealing individual health trajectories or patterns that could be used to identify the user or infer additional health conditions.

title: Excessive Data Processing at Analytics Destination
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) may process or store health log data beyond what is strictly required for health-condition analysis, potentially creating additional data disclosures through derived insights or stored analytics results.

title: Implicit disclosure of location history patterns
description: Location history data transferred from DS2 to P3 enables derivation of daily routine and movement patterns, which may reveal sensitive personal information beyond the explicit data shared. The flow itself represents an implicit disclosure where metadata about movement patterns could be used to link or identify individuals.
assumptions: Location data inherently contains patterns that can reveal sensitive information about daily routines, frequent locations, and behavioral habits.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is a reasonable fit for data disclosure at the flow level, though exact node numbering may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Profiling via inferred health insights
description: Inferred health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags could be used to profile individuals or groups based on health patterns, potentially revealing sensitive group characteristics or enabling inference about individuals' health status beyond what was explicitly shared.
assumptions: The analytics service has access to sufficient historical data to generate meaningful inferences that could be linked to individuals or groups.
uncertainty_note: Using L.2.2.2 from context as it addresses profiling; the exact profiling mechanism depends on the analytics algorithm.

title: Identification through health analytics data sharing
description: The Health Analytics Service shares inferred health insights that are inherently personal data. The act of sharing this data creates a risk that the identity of the data subject can be inferred or deduced from the health-condition risk indicators and trend flags, especially if combined with other data sources.
assumptions: Health analytics outputs are tied to identifiable individuals and the data contains sufficient detail to enable re-identification.
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 is a standard identifying threat node; the specific node may vary based on the exact identification mechanism.

title: Insufficient cybersecurity risk management for health data
description: The Companion Mobile App receives and processes sensitive health analytics data. There is a risk of non-compliance with applicable privacy regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR) due to inadequate cybersecurity risk management practices for handling this sensitive personal data.
assumptions: The app's data handling practices may not meet regulatory requirements for health data protection.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 from context addresses insufficient cybersecurity risk management; actual compliance status depends on the app's implementation.

title: Data Disclosure in Transit - Health Risk Indicators
description: Health risk indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) transmitted from the app to the user could be intercepted or exposed during transmission, potentially leading to unauthorized access to sensitive health information.
assumptions: Data is transmitted over network without adequate encryption or protection
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard mobile app transmission without explicit encryption details

title: Data Disclosure at Destination - User Device Security
description: The user's device may not adequately protect the displayed health risk indicators from local access by others, leading to unauthorized viewing of sensitive health information.
assumptions: User device may lack proper security controls or the user may share device access
uncertainty_note: Assuming typical mobile device usage patterns without specific security configuration details

title: User Unawareness of Health Data Implications
description: The user may not fully understand the implications of the displayed health risk indicators, including potential psychological impact, insurance implications, or how the data could be used by third parties.
assumptions: User may lack medical literacy or awareness of data privacy implications
uncertainty_note: Assuming user may not have full context about health data sensitivity

title: Non-compliance with Health Data Regulations
description: Displaying sensitive health risk indicators may violate health data protection regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR) if proper consent, data minimization, or security measures are not implemented.
assumptions: Health data is subject to regulatory requirements that may not be fully addressed
uncertainty_note: Assuming applicable regulations exist and may not be fully implemented

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Third-Party Cloud Provider
description: Full health and location dataset is transferred to and stored at a third-party cloud hosting provider, constituting explicit disclosure of personal data across a system boundary. This violates the minimality principle as comprehensive datasets are shared rather than only necessary data elements.
assumptions: The cloud provider is a known third party receiving data for hosting purposes.

title: Data in Transit Disclosure Risk
description: Health and location data transmitted in transit to the cloud provider could be intercepted or accessed by unauthorized parties during transmission, leading to unintended disclosure.
assumptions: Data transmission may not be fully encrypted or protected in all scenarios.
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard encryption practices are in place, but transit security should be verified.

title: Identification Risk at Cloud Provider
description: The cloud provider receives full health and location datasets that contain personally identifiable information, creating risk that the provider could identify individuals from the data or use it for purposes beyond the intended analytics.
assumptions: The cloud provider has access to comprehensive personal data including health records and location information.
uncertainty_note: Depends on cloud provider's data handling policies and access controls.

title: Linkability via Metadata
description: Metadata about the data transfer (timing, volume, source/destination) could be used to link individuals or infer patterns about data subjects, even if the data itself is not directly exposed.
assumptions: Metadata about the data flow is observable or accessible to third parties.
uncertainty_note: Assumes metadata is not properly anonymized or protected.
